title: Divisions: writing the quotient and the remainder
header: Divisions: writing the quotient and the remainder

text.text:
### Prerequisites

This text presents an application for practicing division. Before using it, we recommend studying the previous texts in this chapter (<htcite0>), which introduce the multiplication tables and other basic ideas you will need here.

### Practice Reading a text is a good start, but truly understanding division takes practice. In this application, the **Multiplication Tables** menu lets you choose which table to work with. By default it is set to **Randomly**, so a new divisor is chosen each time; if you prefer to focus on a single table, select a number from 1 to 9. The exercise uses the **long division algorithm** (), the step-by-step method for dividing numbers by hand. Remember: when one number does not divide another exactly, the amount that is left over is called the **remainder**. In the following table, we propose dividing one number by another. Write each digit of the quotient in the text boxes. When the digit is correct, the application shows the product of that step; then write the result of the subtraction in the box that appears. As soon as the subtraction is correct, the application moves to the next quotient digit. When you finish, you will receive a medal (). Click the right arrow () to start a new calculation, or click the redo button () to redo the same calculation with the same numbers. The **Division format** buttons let you choose how the division is written: with the **Result below** the bar (as in many schoolbooks) or with the **Result on top** of it (a format that appears in historical mathematical documents).
